title: Landfill geyser erupts at Chiquita Canyon in Castaic, prompts evacuation advisory
text:
Landfill geyser erupts at Chiquita Canyon in Castaic, prompts evacuation advisory - ABC7 Los Angeles 
 24/7 Live Los Angeles Orange County Inland Empire Ventura County California Landfill geyser erupts at Chiquita Canyon in Castaic, prompts evacuation advisory 
 By Michelle Fisher , Madison Weil Tuesday, November 17, 2026 7:32PM 
 A hazardous leak in at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic is now under control after crews capped the source overnight. The leak happened after an explosion of trapped gas shot tons of waste into the air. KABC CASTAIC, Calif. (KABC) -- An explosion of gases sent a thick black geyser shooting into the air above the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic on Monday, prompting an evacuation advisory for nearby residents.
 The Los Angeles County Fire Department responded to the incident in the 29200 block of Henry Mayo Drive around 4 p.m.
 The plume, visible for miles, rose about 500 feet into the air and was accompanied by a noxious odor. Black smoke billowed into the air before turning white.
 An explosion of gases sent a thick black geyser shooting into the air above the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic. 
 The city of Santa Clarita advised residents to avoid the area near Henry Mayo Drive and Highway 126. An evacuation advisory was issued for several zones, including CAS-VALVERDE-A, CAS-HASLEY, CAS-HILLCREST, CAS-CAMBRIDGE, CAS-INDUSTRY and CAS-LIVEOAK.
 L.A. County Fire Department officials sought to reassure residents as hazardous materials teams monitored air quality.
 "No one is at risk. We wouldn't be standing here without respiratory devices if there was any sort of risk," L.A. County Fire Department Capt. Aaron Katon told reporters.
 According to fire officials, the eruption occurred during routine drilling operations intended to vent the landfill. Crews working in an area that had not been addressed in some time struck an underground deposit of gases, triggering the release.
 At least four workers were taken to a hospital for evaluation as a precaution, according to the fire department.
 By Monday night, the plume had diminished significantly and changed from black to white. First responders said they were not concerned about a secondary gas explosion.
 Fire officials said crews had capped the leak by 11 p.m. and that it was no longer off-gassing. Hazardous materials teams planned to remain at the site overnight to continue monitoring air quality.
 In a statement, Chiquita Canyon said, "During a routine drilling operation to install a new well at Chiquita Canyon Landfill to help address the elevated temperature landfill event, crews encountered a pressurized pocket within the landfill, resulting in an above-ground release of gases and particulate material at the drilling location. No liquids were released. Work was stopped immediately and the area has been secured. Chiquita is in communication and coordinating with state and local regulatory agencies and emergency response personnel."

 "As a precaution, Chiquita Canyon is reviewing data from all local air quality monitoring equipment."
 The incident renewed attention on the landfill, three weeks after California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against its owners alleging a pattern of hazardous waste violations.
 Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger said she was "not pleased" by the incident.
 "The families of Castaic and the surrounding communities have lived with the burden of this landfill for far too long, and they should not have to wonder whether they are safe," Barger said in a statement. "I want answers, and I will not accept vague explanations."
 Barger told Eyewitness News she believes the incident reflects mismanagement rather than a mishap.
 "This has got to be addressed, and that's why the county filed a lawsuit to require Chiquita to provide financial resources for those who want to relocate," she said. "People shouldn't have to live in fear."
 L.A. County public health officials have issued a directive to the operators of the Chiquita Canyon Landfill to immediately offer relocation assistance to community members affected by the incident.
 "The LA County Fire Department continues to monitor air quality with no hazardous findings currently. However, the resulting strong odors from the November 16 incident may cause headaches, nausea, dizziness, and irritation of the eyes, nose, or throat," the L.A. County Department of Public Health said in a statement.
 The health department recommends that impacted residents reduce exposure, consider temporary relocation and pay attention to symptoms.
